tasks.short: Check every animal on the round, look closer at those that seem unwell, note concerns and call the vet.

steps.what: Caretaker observes each animal on the morning round
Caretaker examines animals that seem unwell for signs of illness or injury
Caretaker writes concerns: on the paper kennel card today, on a tablet in the animal care record with a photo after the change
Caretaker phones the vet about sick animals

tasks.design: Nothing changes in this task's time. Observing, examining and calling the vet stay fully with the caretaker, and the concern note is the caretaker's own first record: written on a tablet in the shelter's animal care record ({OTHER}) with a photo instead of on the kennel card, it takes as long, but the next shift and the vet see it at once. No software judges an animal's health.
tasks.previous_blocker: Concerns were written on kennel cards that only people at that kennel saw.
tasks.enabler_now: Care records on tablets are standard in shelters and kennels.
tasks.still_hard: Spotting illness is skill and attention; only a vet may diagnose.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing the cat that is quieter than yesterday.

reach.learn: Whether photo notes speed up the vet's triage.

evidence.claim: Animal care records on tablets hold notes and photos per animal.
Examining animals to diagnose and treat is reserved for vets; caretakers observe and report.

assumptions: Boundary: from the round to the vet called; treatment is outside.
Input contract: animal records created at intake by the shelter office; fallback is kennel cards.
Every step keeps its full time; s3 is a first record, and writing it on a tablet takes as long as on the card.
No camera or sensor monitoring is added.
research_questions: Do vets act sooner on photo notes?

incremental.description: No new work: the note replaces the kennel card entry.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: No time saving in this task: observing, examining, calling the vet and the caretaker's own concern notes keep their full time; the gain is that notes are shared at once.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Weigh and measure animals, record intake and condition, copy cards into the system, tick medicines given, flag missed doses and weight loss, and follow up with the vet.

steps.what: Caretaker weighs and measures the animals
Caretaker records weight, physical condition and food intake: on paper kennel cards today, on a tablet in the animal care record after the change
Caretaker copies the kennel cards into the shelter system at the end of the day
Caretaker records medications given against the vet's prescription
Caretaker goes through the cards for missed doses and weight changes
Caretaker follows up alerts with the shelter vet by phone

tasks.design: Weights, condition, food intake and doses are entered on a tablet in the shelter's animal care record ({OTHER}) instead of on cards, which takes as long, so the record is complete without copying cards at night. The vet's prescription shows as a dose list to tick, and a rule alerts the caretaker to a missed dose or a weight drop above a set percentage; weighing and calling the vet stay manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Kennel cards were filled in by hand and copied into the system at the end of the day.
tasks.enabler_now: Care records on tablets hold pick lists, dose lists and simple alert rules.
tasks.still_hard: Entries must be made at the kennel, not from memory; alerts only fire on recorded data.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing that a dog eating half its food is, for this dog, a warning sign.

reach.learn: Whether complete records shorten vet rounds.

evidence.claim: Animal care records support pick lists, dose lists and alert rules.
Prescribing treatment is reserved for vets; caretakers give prescribed medicines and record them.

assumptions: Boundary: from weighing to vet follow-up; treatment is outside.
Input contract: prescriptions entered by the shelter vet; alert thresholds set by the vet; animal records from intake; fallback is kennel cards.
Vet time is outside the caretaker's savings.

Weighing, recording care entries and vet calls keep their full time; entries are the caretaker's own first record. s3 drops because nothing is copied at night. s4 keeps 60 because the vet's prescription fills medicine and dose and the caretaker ticks each dose given. s5 drops because the rule flags missed doses and weight drops; the caretaker reviews each alert (new work).
research_questions: Do missed doses fall with dose lists and alerts?

incremental.description: Caretaker reviews each alert before calling.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: half of the kennels have no tablet at the pens, so their cards are still copied and searched; s3 and s5 keep 50 (20.5); high: tablets at every pen (35.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Answer calls, check free kennels, write phone bookings, take in online bookings, confirm bookings and schedule adoption visits.

steps.what: Owners book a kennel or an adoption visit online, typing their own details
Caretaker answers telephones about availability, prices and adoption
Caretaker checks free kennels in the paper diary while the caller waits
Caretaker writes phone bookings: in the paper diary today, typed into the booking system after the change
Caretaker copies e-mailed booking requests into the diary
Caretaker checks each phone booking before it is confirmed: dates, kennel, animal and the owner's e-mail address
Caretaker phones owners to confirm their bookings
Caretaker schedules appointments for adoption visits by e-mail

tasks.design: The kennel's website shows live availability and prices from the booking system ({OTHER}) and takes bookings, which land in the system directly, so fewer owners need to call. Phone bookings are typed into the same system and checked by the caretaker, every booking gets an automatic confirmation, and adoption visits are booked through a link with the coordinator's free slots; calls that remain are answered in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Availability lived in a paper diary, so every question and booking came by phone or e-mail.
tasks.enabler_now: Booking systems with live availability and automatic confirmations are standard.
tasks.still_hard: Many owners phone to talk about their animal, not only to book.
tasks.human_edge: Reassuring an owner who is nervous about leaving their dog.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; routine calls fall away.

evidence.claim: Booking systems show live availability, take online bookings and send confirmations.
Owner contact data are personal data; animal health data are not a special category.

assumptions: Boundary: from the call to the confirmed booking or visit; the stay itself is outside.
Input contract: kennels, prices and the coordinator's free slots kept by the kennel manager; fallback is the paper diary.
Owner time is outside the caretaker's savings.

Calls that remain are answered as now, and the check of each phone booking keeps its full time. s1 and s3 keep 60 because about 40% of owners book online (s1o, owner time). s2 keeps 30 for looking up free kennels in the system. s6 keeps 50 because adopters pick a slot through the link.
unknowns: Share of bookings that would move online.
research_questions: How many calls per day disappear once availability is online?

incremental.description: Caretaker checks online bookings each morning.
Kennel manager keeps prices and availability rules current.

approvals.approved_version: Each phone booking with dates, kennel, animal and owner's e-mail exactly as checked by the caretaker in s3c; the booking system sends its confirmation once to that owner. Online bookings are confirmed as the owner entered them. Any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: most owners prefer to phone, so only about 15% book online; s1 and s3 keep 85 and s6 keeps 80 (44.4); high: about 40% book online (59.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Advise owners in person, route e-mailed symptom questions to the vet, answer care questions from vetted sheets, send care sheets to new owners and remind owners of vaccinations.

steps.what: Caretaker advises pet owners at pick-up and adoption on how to care for their pets' health
Caretaker reads e-mailed questions to spot those that need the vet
Caretaker answers owners' e-mailed care questions: writes from memory today; reads a drafted reply that quotes the vetted care sheet after the change

loop.input: An owner's e-mailed question that the red-flag rules did not send to the vet, and the vetted care sheets per species.
loop.output: A draft reply that names the species and topic and quotes the matching care sheet passage with its link.
loop.check: Code checks the reply quotes a sheet passage word for word and contains no medicine, dose or diagnosis; any question mentioning symptoms, medicines or doses goes to the vet unanswered. The caretaker reads each draft against the owner's question and checks that the quoted passage answers it for that species; if not, they write the reply or pass it to the vet.
loop.stop: One draft per question; no matching sheet means the caretaker writes or forwards it.
loop.why_not_simpler: Owners ask in their own words; a keyword search misses species and topic too often.

steps.what: Caretaker checks the final reply: it answers the question, quotes the right species sheet, holds no medical advice, and goes to the right owner
Caretaker sends the checked reply to the owner
Shelter vet answers questions about symptoms and medicines
Caretaker checks the care sheets before they go: the animal's species and name, and the new owner's address
Caretaker prints care sheets for new owners
Caretaker checks the vaccination and worming dates in the animal record and the new owner's contact details at adoption
Caretaker phones owners to remind them of vaccination and worming dates

tasks.design: Red-flag rules send any e-mailed question about symptoms, medicines or doses straight to the shelter vet's queue. For the rest, a bounded step drafts a reply that quotes the vetted national care sheets per species, and the caretaker reads it against the question, checks the final reply and sends it. After the caretaker checks them, care sheets go to new owners from the animal's record, and the record sends vaccination and worming reminders on the dates the caretaker checked at adoption; advice at the desk stays in person and no chatbot talks to owners.
tasks.previous_blocker: Every e-mail was answered from memory and reminders were phoned.
tasks.enabler_now: Independent, vetted care information per species exists, and language models can match free text to a topic.
tasks.still_hard: The line between care advice and diagnosis must hold; wrong advice can harm an animal and expose the shelter.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing in a worried owner's question that the animal needs a vet today.
tasks.altitude: The caretaker checks quoted replies; medical questions go to the vet.

reach.learn: Whether quoted sheets keep advice consistent.

evidence.claim: A national centre gives independent care, health and welfare advice per pet species.
Examining and prescribing for animals is reserved for vets; staff may give general care advice.
A tribunal held an airline liable for its chatbot's wrong advice; quoted answers must match the source word for word.

assumptions: Boundary: from owners' questions to replies and reminders; veterinary treatment is outside.
Input contract: care sheets from the national information centre, used with its terms; red-flag word list set by the shelter vet; care dates from the animal record; fallback is answering from memory.
Vet time is outside the caretaker's savings.

Advice in person and every check before a reply, care sheet or reminder goes keep their full time. s3 keeps 50 because the draft quotes the sheet and the caretaker reads it against the question; s2 drops because the red-flag rules route symptom questions to the vet.
research_questions: How many owner questions are matched to a care sheet?

already_counted.description: Caretaker reads every drafted reply before sending.

incremental.description: Caretaker forwards questions the rules miss to the vet.
Shelter vet keeps the red-flag list current.

approvals.approved_version: The vaccination and worming dates and the owner's contact details exactly as checked by the caretaker in s7; the record sends each reminder once to that owner on the date due. Any change in dates or owner needs a new check.
The vetted care sheets for the animal's species with its name, exactly as checked by the caretaker in s5c, sent once from the animal's record to the new owner's address; any change needs a new check.
The reply text exactly as checked by the caretaker in s3c, sent once by e-mail to the owner who asked; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many e-mailed questions fall outside the care sheets, so the caretaker writes most replies and s3 keeps 80 (36.8); high: most questions match a sheet (44.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The animal caretaker keeps the animals' daily care and the conversations with owners; cards, diaries and reminder calls go.
skills_to_grow: Spotting questions that need the vet
role.ambitious_version: A caretaker who spends the day with the animals while records, bookings and reminders run themselves.
